attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, in his authorial voice. The Fitch quote that follows is separate.

semantics.note: Faithful. It pairs a present-tense judgement with a firm 'no amount... will' prediction that has no deadline. Treating it as a forecast is reasonable.

contract.note: The categorical reading of 'no amount... will fix' is the ordinary one. It is fair to exclude the uses he concedes (coding, search, brainstorming, documents). The speaker gives no task list, threshold or deadline, so the evaluator had to choose these.

evidence.note: The Kenyan clinical RCT ran Apr–Jul 2025, before the post. It shows no benefit in one setting, but it cannot show that future investment will fail.
Reliability of one deployed agent improved from March to August 2026. There is no full-cost economics and no link to added investment, so the contradiction condition is not met.
This benchmark framework measures oversight and cost. The case study does not show real-world economic viability for the promised tasks.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm, open-ended prediction that investment will not fix LLMs' unsuitability. No item in the packet is a post-publication deployment showing reliable, cost-justified performance beyond the conceded uses. Finite failures cannot prove permanent impossibility. With no deadline, the claim remains unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. The Suresh quote that follows is a separate source and is not used.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'hard to tell' caveat, the 'most of those costs' scope and the Twitter exception. The caveat hedges usefulness, but the denial that the tools have enhanced people is stated firmly.

contract.note: It is an ordinary reading that 'yet to substantively... enhance' denies any demonstrated meaningful gain in real work beyond testimonials, and that 'yet' makes it cumulative to the post date. The usefulness caveat creates some tension but does not soften the firm denial.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed field RCTs with 4,867 developers found 26% more completed tasks. It was published Feb 2026, before the post: meaningful workplace enhancement beyond testimonials.
METR's 2025 RCT found experienced developers 19% slower. It supports the claim in that setting only and cannot show enhancement never happened anywhere.
METR's own follow-up shows weak signs of a speedup but calls its estimate unreliable. Neither side can rely on it.

reviews.rationale: The blanket claim that the tools have not enhanced people is contradicted by e1, a large peer-reviewed field study published before the post that found substantial gains in completed tasks. A slowdown in one smaller study does not save a categorical claim. The cost clauses ('very expensive', most costs hidden or subsidised) have no evidence either way. The contract allows contradiction through the enhancement clause alone.

attribution.note: Zitron's own flat assertion in his post.

semantics.note: A universal present-tense claim, rendered verbatim. It is hyperbolic in context but firm in form.

contract.note: The ordinary reading (no AI-first startup earns a company-wide net profit) is fair. Choosing Q1 2026 is an evaluator decision. The rule that an unknown accounting basis blocks any score is generous to the speaker; one well-documented profitable startup would ordinarily refute the claim.

evidence.note: Secondary summary of the founder's own disclosure calling Midjourney profitable. No profit measure, no accounts and no Q1 2026 figure, so it falls short of the contradiction condition. It weighs against the claim, though.

reviews.rationale: A universal 'every' claim would fall to one credible counterexample. The only one in the packet is a secondary report of Midjourney's self-described profitability, with no defined measure or period. That is a company disclosure, not matched financial evidence for the target quarter, so the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the lab-loss clause and the 'never, ever' recovery forecast. It drops the side claim that startups and enterprise customers lose money paying per token; that clause is not graded here. A compound claim whose horizon is set by the forecast.

contract.note: Reasonable readings: a $20B+ collective annual loss in calendar 2025, and 'never' as unrecovered lifetime GPU investment. Basis matters: net losses include large fair-value charges. Support for the forecast needs a closed investment lifecycle.

evidence.note: Audited S-1 filed before the evaluation date: Anthropic's 2025 net loss was $42.0B, of which $34.3B was fair-value changes. This supports the loss clause on a GAAP net basis only; it says nothing on recovery.
Reports OpenAI's 2025 net loss near $39B and operating loss of $20.92B. This supports the loss clause; it is secondary reporting on leaked documents.
S&P's outlook expects better monetisation and positive cash flow from 2029. This is a forecast, not realised recovery, and it measures broad capex.

reviews.rationale: The loss clause looks supported: reported 2025 net losses are about $42B (Anthropic) and $39B (OpenAI), and OpenAI's operating loss alone is $20.9B. Large fair-value charges make the result basis-dependent. The 'never' recovery forecast has no deadline, and no closed lifecycle or verified recovery appears in the evidence, so the overall claim is unresolved.
